FT reports Capstone was also linked to a separate case where stolen cash from elderly victims was allegedly converted into USDT.

Tether and Bitfinex said they were EQIBank customers, but had no knowledge of Capstone’s alleged misconduct.

This highlights Tether’s banking access problem, relying on smaller offshore banks and payment middlemen to reach the dollar system.

Meta’s AI Tax Bonanza: Billions Saved as Washington Pays the Bill


Meta is pouring billions of dollars into the infrastructure behind the artificial-intelligence boom. At the same time, the company has found a powerful way to reduce its federal tax bill: using tax incentives designed to encourage investment in research, development and capital infrastructure.

The result is striking. Meta reported a federal income-tax rate of just over 3.5% for 2025, its lowest rate since Facebook went public. Its federal tax bill fell to roughly $2.8 billion, compared with about $9.6 billion the previous year, even as its domestic profits climbed to roughly $79.6 billion.

Meta is not alone. Amazon and Alphabet also reported sharply lower tax bills as they accelerated spending on AI infrastructure, servers, chips and data centers. 

Amazon’s federal tax bill fell from about $9 billion in 2024 to roughly $1.2 billion in 2025, while Alphabet’s combined federal and state tax figure declined from about $21.1 billion to $13.8 billion.

Much of the change is linked to the tax legislation signed by President Donald Trump in 2025. The law expanded or restored deductions allowing companies to write off certain capital investments and research expenses more quickly. For technology companies racing to build enormous AI computing networks, those provisions can translate into billions of dollars in tax savings or deferred payments.

Meta’s AI expansion is therefore doing double duty: increasing the company’s computing capacity while generating expenses that can reduce its taxable income.

There is, however, an important distinction. Lower taxes today do not necessarily mean those taxes disappear forever. Some provisions effectively push tax payments into future years. Meta reported more than $18 billion in deferred taxes for 2025.

Supporters argue that accelerated deductions encourage companies to invest in American technology, infrastructure and research rather than shifting those investments overseas. Critics counter that the incentives are increasingly benefiting some of the world’s most profitable corporations on a massive scale.

The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy estimates that Meta, Amazon and Alphabet collectively reduced their federal tax payments by nearly $50 billion in 2025 compared with what they would have owed at the statutory 21% corporate rate.

That is an advocacy group’s calculation, rather than an amount determined by the IRS.

The controversy is about more than accounting. AI data centers have become one of the biggest engines of corporate investment, with individual facilities costing billions of dollars. They also consume enormous amounts of electricity and, depending on their cooling systems, significant quantities of water.

That leaves Washington facing a difficult question: when Congress creates tax breaks to stimulate innovation, where is the line between encouraging investment and subsidizing the expansion of already enormously profitable technology companies?

For Meta, the answer is increasingly visible in its balance sheet. The company is spending aggressively on AI — and the tax code is helping make that expansion substantially cheaper.

🔔 South Korea targets November review for second stage crypto legislation 

🌐 South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has set November for a National Assembly subcommittee review of the Digital Asset Framework Act, rejecting claims that work on the country’s second stage crypto legislation has been delayed. According to Seo Na yoon, head of the FSC’s virtual asset division, the regulator and lawmakers are moving in the same direction on legislation covering digital asset issuance and distribution, including stablecoins. Speaking at a National Assembly seminar in Seoul on Sept. 22, Seo said differences remain over when the government will submit its draft, but the November review remains part of the planned timetable. 

⚡️ “The FSC is not dragging its feet at all. We share the same view,” Seo said, responding to criticism over the pace of the legislation. “The direction has already been set, and while detailed discussions may be necessary in the process, there is certainly no intention on the FSC’s part to delay.”

🔗 Seo said the regulator wants the legislation passed quickly and expects discussions to proceed using bills that lawmakers have already introduced alongside the government’s proposal. Ten digital asset and stablecoin bills are currently pending in the National Assembly, giving lawmakers existing proposals to work from before the government completes its version.
